must_not_claim.why_dangerous: PEP is highly but not 100% effective — false certainty leads to risk behaviour
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: PEP is highly effective when started promptly and completed fully but does not guarantee prevention

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: PEP can be started after 72 hours
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: after 72 hours PEP is not recommended as effectiveness drops sharply
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: PEP must be started within 72 hours — after this window it is no longer recommended

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: PrEP is appropriate for everyone
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: PrEP requires HIV negative status and ongoing adherence assessment — not universally appropriate
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: PrEP is appropriate for people at ongoing high risk — a health provider will assess your eligibility

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: PEP and PrEP are the same medication or approach
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: different drugs, different timing, different indications — conflation causes dangerous misuse
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: PEP and PrEP are different — PEP is emergency use after exposure, PrEP is preventive use before exposure

context_terms.usage_note: central term — always specify what type of exposure: unprotected sex, assault, needlestick
cluster 0 questions may involve assault context — handle with sensitivity and include GBV resource referral
critical for both PEP and PrEP effectiveness — missed doses reduce efficacy

diverge_terms.register_triggered: conflation with morning-after pill — completely different intervention
diverge_terms.safer_alternative: be explicit: PEP prevents HIV not pregnancy — emergency contraception is separate

diverge_terms.register_triggered: clinical jargon — accessible if defined
diverge_terms.safer_alternative: introduce as 'HIV prevention medication called antiretrovirals (ART)' then use ART abbreviation

cross_cutting_flags.flag: always state the 72-hour window prominently and urgently
cross_cutting_flags.reason: time criticality is the single most important fact in PEP — delays are irreversible
cross_cutting_flags.implementation: 72-hour window must be the first clinical fact stated in every PEP answer

cross_cutting_flags.flag: always distinguish PEP from PrEP in the same answer
cross_cutting_flags.reason: only 39 rows in this cluster — many questions conflate the two
cross_cutting_flags.implementation: define both PEP and PrEP with their timing difference in every G11 answer even if only one is asked about

must_have_terms.verbose_form: sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections passed from one person to another through sexual contact
the only reliable way to know if you have an STI is to get tested at a health facility — symptoms alone are not enough
there are many different types of STIs including chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, herpes, HIV, and HPV — each requires different treatment
many STIs cause no symptoms — a person can have an STI and feel completely healthy while still able to transmit it
using condoms correctly and consistently reduces the risk of most STIs significantly
visit a health facility for testing, diagnosis, and treatment — do not self-diagnose or self-treat
if you are diagnosed with an STI, all recent sexual partners must be notified and encouraged to get tested

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: a specific STI diagnosis based on described symptoms
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: multiple STIs share symptoms — only testing provides diagnosis
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: these symptoms could indicate an STI — get tested at a health facility for an accurate diagnosis

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: STIs only affect certain types of people
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: cluster 42 is specifically about STIs in boys and women — stigma-free framing required
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: STIs can affect anyone who is sexually active regardless of gender, age, or relationship type

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: STIs are always obvious or visible
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: most STIs are asymptomatic — false confidence leads to untested infections
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: most STIs cause no visible symptoms — regular testing is the only reliable way to know your status

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: treating one STI protects against others
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: false — each STI requires its own treatment and protection
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: treating one STI does not protect against others — condoms and regular testing are needed for all STIs

context_terms.usage_note: neutral term covering vaginal, oral, and anal routes — use over 'sex' when possible for clinical precision
cluster 42 specifically addresses STIs in boys — gender-inclusive framing matters
cluster 42 also addresses women — use alongside boy/man for inclusive coverage

diverge_terms.register_triggered: stigma/moral register — completely inappropriate
diverge_terms.safer_alternative: STIs are medical conditions — remove any moral framing from answers

diverge_terms.register_triggered: stigma register
diverge_terms.safer_alternative: never use 'dirty' in relation to STIs or people with STIs — replace with clinical neutral language

diverge_terms.register_triggered: moral judgement register
diverge_terms.safer_alternative: use 'multiple sexual partners' as a neutral risk factor descriptor

cross_cutting_flags.flag: never name a specific STI as the diagnosis without testing context
cross_cutting_flags.reason: G12 is for general STI questions — specific diagnosis requires testing and is outside scope
cross_cutting_flags.implementation: always add 'testing is needed for an accurate diagnosis' when symptom questions arise

cross_cutting_flags.flag: always name at least 3 common STIs to illustrate variety
cross_cutting_flags.reason: patients asking general STI questions benefit from understanding the breadth of the category
cross_cutting_flags.implementation: list 3 examples: chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis as the minimum named examples

must_have_terms.verbose_form: prayer, fasting, and holy water cannot cure a bacterial, viral, or parasitic infection — these are medical conditions requiring medical treatment
this condition requires medical treatment from a health provider — spiritual practices alone are not sufficient
please visit your nearest health facility as soon as possible for testing and medical treatment
your faith and spiritual practices are respected and can provide comfort and strength alongside medical treatment
delaying medical treatment while relying solely on spiritual remedies allows the infection to progress and cause serious harm
many people find strength in combining their faith with medical treatment — these approaches can work together
without medical treatment this infection can cause serious complications including infertility, organ damage, or death

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: spiritual practices are useless or invalid
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: dismissing faith alienates the patient and reduces likelihood of following medical advice — cultural respect is clinically essential
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: acknowledge faith respectfully while clearly stating that medical treatment is also needed

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: prayer or holy water could have partial effectiveness
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: any validation of the myth delays medical treatment
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: be clear that the condition cannot be treated without medicine, while respecting the person's faith

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: the traditional healer or pastor is wrong to recommend this
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: attacking trusted community figures creates resistance and damages the clinical relationship
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: focus on what the medical evidence shows rather than criticising the source of the belief

must_not_claim.forbidden_claim: this condition is a spiritual punishment
must_not_claim.why_dangerous: reinforces harmful stigma and prevents health-seeking
must_not_claim.safe_alternative: frame the condition as a medical issue with a medical solution — spiritual framing of illness as punishment is never appropriate

context_terms.usage_note: appears in cluster questions — reference respectfully without dismissing
common in Uganda and Ghana contexts — respected community figure, do not dismiss
specific to clusters 52 and 75 — handle with cultural sensitivity
specific to cluster 45 — common religious practice in Ethiopia and Uganda contexts
use as positive term for spiritual belief — distinct from the specific remedy being addressed

diverge_terms.register_triggered: dismissive/condescending register — will alienate patient
diverge_terms.safer_alternative: never use superstition — use 'this belief' or 'this approach' neutrally

diverge_terms.register_triggered: condescending register
diverge_terms.safer_alternative: never imply the patient is uneducated for holding a traditional belief

diverge_terms.register_triggered: confrontational register when directed at belief systems
diverge_terms.safer_alternative: use 'medical evidence shows' or 'this condition requires' rather than 'that belief is wrong'

cross_cutting_flags.flag: mandatory 3-step structure: acknowledge → clarify → redirect
cross_cutting_flags.reason: this is the unique answer structure requirement for all cultural myth questions — standard clinical QA structure fails here
cross_cutting_flags.implementation: Step 1: acknowledge the belief respectfully ('many people turn to prayer and traditional remedies'). Step 2: clarify the clinical limitation ('this condition is caused by [virus/bacteria/parasite] which requires medical treatment'). Step 3: redirect urgently ('please visit a health facility as soon as possible for treatment that can prevent serious complications')

cross_cutting_flags.flag: always include urgency framing
cross_cutting_flags.reason: patients asking these questions may have been delaying treatment for some time — urgency is clinically critical
cross_cutting_flags.implementation: include 'as soon as possible' or 'without delay' in every G13 answer

cross_cutting_flags.flag: country-specific cultural calibration
cross_cutting_flags.reason: holy water framing is more common in Ethiopian Orthodox context; pastoral/prayer framing in Uganda/Ghana Pentecostal context — answer register should reflect this
cross_cutting_flags.implementation: for Amh_Eth questions: reference Orthodox spiritual practice context. For Eng_Uga/Lug_Uga/Aka_Gha questions: reference pastoral/evangelical context. For Swa_Ken: both Christian and Islamic framing may appear.
